overview: This bill adds about 5,600 acres of the George Washington National Forest in Virginia to two existing federal wilderness areas. Wilderness is the strictest level of protection for public land: roads, motor vehicles, logging and new development are generally not allowed. About 1,000 acres would be added right away to the Rough Mountain Wilderness. About 4,600 acres next to the Rich Hole Wilderness would first be treated as "potential wilderness" so the Forest Service can finish planned work to improve water quality and fish passage using machinery, then become full wilderness when that work is done or after five years, whichever comes first. As of October 27, 2025, the bill had been approved by a Senate committee and placed on the Senate's calendar.
for: Supporters say the bill permanently protects forest land that the Forest Service's own plan already recommended for wilderness, while still letting planned stream restoration work be finished first.
against: Critics say wilderness status permanently rules out uses such as motorized recreation, road building and timber management on the added land, limiting future flexibility to manage the forest.
